messages.subject: RE: [geomorph-r-package] bilat.symmetry vs. procD.lm results?
messages.body_plain:
Natasha,

There were two implementation errors in your example that caused the discrepancies.

First, because this is a nested model, one must specify the ‘ind:side’ as the error for the main effects of ‘ind’ and ‘side’ for your procD.lm approach.  This will generate the proper F-values, effect sizes, and p-values

Second, your use of bilat.symmetry was not quite correct. Notice in the help file that if one performs GPA prior to running bilat.symmetry, then one provides bilat.symmetry with the gpagen object, not its components. You provided the components, meaning that another gpagen was performed within bilat.symmetry: resulting in slight rotational differences (and thus the SS differences in the 3rd or 4th digit).

Here is your example again, with corrected code. Note now that the methods yield identical results.

data(mosquito)

Y.gpa <- gpagen(mosquito$wingshape)

gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = Y.gpa$coords,

                           ind = mosquito$ind, #for some reason, "individual" or "critter" didn't work, only "ind" did.

                           side = mosquito$side,

                           replicate = mosquito$rep)

## NOTE what one puts in 'A'

wing.sym <- bilat.symmetry(A = Y.gpa, ind = ind, side=side,data = gdf,

                           object.sym = FALSE)

wing.anova<-procD.lm(shape ~ ind + side + ind/side, data= gdf)

wing.sym$shape.anova

## NOTE specification of error terms for main effects

anova(wing.anova, error = c("ind:side", "ind:side","Residuals"))

messages.body_plain:
Fatih,

Whether one uses PLS or regression depends on the nature of the variables you are associating with shape, as well as the hypothesis. PLS describes covariation between sets of variables, while linear models allow for predictions of how shape changes with one or more dependent variables.

For all of these, one can generate TPS deformation grids using the ‘shape.predictor’ function in geomorph. The help file provides examples for shape predictions from PCA, regression, anova, PLS and I think a few others.

To your last question, differences between males and females is an anova question; also attained via linear models.

Best,

Dean

Dear all,

I have a question on how to interpret the outcome of a phylogenetic 2B-PLS using the phylo.integration function.
Input is (1) a matrix containing shape coordinates for the distal ulna and (2) another matrix containing results on maximal range of motion of the wrist during ulnar deviation. I include a phylogenetic tree, and to match the tips of the tree (i.e. one datapoint per tip) the matrices above obviously contain mean shapes and mean range of motion.

When looking at the plot, I find it strange how the red regression line is drawn ... Judging from the datapoints, I would expect it to be more in between "Nomascus" and "Hylobates" on the right side, no? What does the analysis take into account to calculate this line?

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] phylogenetic 2B-PLS (phylo.integration) - strange result
messages.body_plain:
Dear Marie,

The line is a best-fit line based on least-squares.  It is not “drawn” to match any perception of how it should be drawn.  It is exactly what it is, the line that minimizes squared distances of points to it.

It appears that Pan paniscus has a lot of leverage.  You could remove this species, re-run the analysis, check the line as well as the r-PLS statistical results and if it appears everything improves in a way that heartens your perception, you know this species is something of an outlier, and investigation into why should be biologically interesting.  What is it about Pan paniscus that causes this species to have an association between ulna shape and function that bucks the trend you see in other primates?

It could also simply be that there is not much association between ulna shape and range of motion in the primates you sampled.  There does not have to be a pattern.

Best,

Mike

messages.subject: Re: [geomorph-r-package] align2procSym
messages.body_plain:
Dear Rebeka,

This is a bit of a challenging question to answer because alignment without scaling to unit size is actually not GPA and cannot be considered GPA.  The reason for this is that in the rotation step it would not be rotation if the configurations are not the same size — it would be a shear, thus changing the spatial relationship among the points of a landmark configuration.  If you are interested in something like boas coordinates, you can simply multiply Procrustes coordinates from your sample of species 1 times their centroid sizes to inflate the unit configurations back to their original size.

I think this is what you had in mind — that is actually the simpler way — but contriving the GPA to not scale configurations to centroid size would be tantamount to allowing shears rather than rotation, which is a bit of chicanery you might wish to avoid.

I hope that makes sense.  If not, please let me know and i will go into further detail.

Mike

messages.body_plain:
Regarding the request below,

> On Mar 10, 2023, at 4:30 PM, Mgr. Rebeka Rmoutilová <rebeka.v...@natur.cuni.cz> wrote:
>
> I don't know how to align the specimens of species 2 on the PCA performed with species 1. Could you please help me with that?

if you perform GPA with gpagen in geomorph, then multiply the $coords times the $Csize output to acquire adjusted data for species 1, you can concatenate that data with those from species 2 and perform GPA again to align species 2 data with that of species 1 data, aligned to PC axes of species 1.  In the second step simply choose PrinAxes = FALSE to not re-align to PC axes after aligning to the first PC of species 1.

Best,
Mike

Hello,

I am trying to compare a few different possible models for explaining my data with procD.pgls (mainly trying to see if incorporating size leads to a significantly better model), and along the way discovered that some of my variables flip flop between being significant and non-significant (sometimes by quite a bit) depending on the model. I abbreviate the r output below for a few examples, with P-values bolded. Any thoughts on whether this should be expected and possible recommendations for interpreting and choosing the most meaningful model?

When I incorporate a model that just includes diet as an independent variable it is very insignificant:

> summary(procD.pgls(coords ~ Diet, phy=phy, data=allo_notroph, SS.type="III"))

           Df      SS        MS     Rsq      F        Z Pr(>F)
Diet        9 0.01282 0.0014249 0.01845 0.2882 -0.96077  0.839

> summary(procD.pgls(coords ~ Diet*Habitat_Use*log(cs), phy=phy, data=allo_notroph, SS.type="III"))

Diet                       9 0.00963 0.00106994 0.013853 1.3791 1.31152  0.104
Habitat_Use                6 0.00577 0.00096187 0.008302 1.2398 0.86122  0.188
log(cs)                    1 0.00208 0.00207874 0.002990 2.6794 1.96679  0.034 *

Greg

messages.body_plain:
Greg,

It is impossible to provide a stock answer to whether or not what you observe with Diet “is expected” for all situations. What I can say is that one’s intuition as to whether the ‘strength’ of effect explained by a factor when included in various models is not as straight forward as the post implies. To truly understand what is expected, one must consider both the full (hypothesis) model, and its reduced model(s); the latter of which also changes based on the sums-of-squares types one chooses to use.

Consider your example. You have models like:

Shape ~ diet

Shape ~ diet + many things

Shape ~ diet + many (some other) things

These define your full(hypothesis) models, and are fine.  Now, the other critical thing to consider is that you are using marginal (type III) SS.  This defines the reduced models for each term in your model.  Recall that type III SS are ‘exclusion-based’; meaning that the importance of a variable in terms of its SS is calculated by subtraction: what component of SS changes when that variable is removed from the model, given that the rest of the explanatory variables remain in the model.

So to your example you have (shape = Y for simplicity below):

FULL                                      REDUCED

Y ~ diet                                 Y ~ 1

Y ~ diet + many                 Y ~ many

Y ~ diet + many.2             Y ~ many.2

Thus, the effect of diet is evaluated relative to the overall mean model, or a model including many, or including many.2.  That could change a great deal, depending upon what is in ‘many’.  This is what you observed.

Was this surprising? Not really. It is only surprising if one has the expectation that the effect of a term in a model is unchanged across models (i.e,. ignores the reduced model against which it is compared).

I suggest a careful read of statistical theory on sums-of-squares, what they do and don’t tell us, how they are calculated, and of course the literature on model comparison. This might help one’s intuition match what the math is revealing.

Best,

Dean

messages.body_plain:
Fatih,

There are two ways to do this. One is visual, and one is more statistical.

First, since each relationship is a regression of shape ~ other, one could generate predicted shapes along each regression (e.g., using shape.predictor) and compare these visually for both regressions to see whether shape changes are similar.

Second, this could be accompanied by calculating the angle between vectors of regression coefficients. If this angle is small, it implies the regressions are oriented in similar directions, and hence shape changes implied by these are similar. A permutation test could be used to evaluate this angle.

Dean

Dear geomorph community,

I have three separate questions on the coefficients, residuals, and speed of lm.rrpp.

Question 1:
Using the pupfish data, I compared coefficient estimation for log(CS) and sex from a joint fit (the fit object below) and a two-stage fit (using residuals from fit1 as dependent variables for fit2):

library(geomorph)

data(Pupfish)

Y.gpa<-gpagen(pupfish$coords, print.progress = FALSE)

gdf1 <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = as.matrix(two.d.array(Y.gpa$coords)), CS = Pupfish$CS, Sex = Pupfish$Sex)
fit <- lm.rrpp(shape ~ log(CS) + Sex, SS.type = "I",
               data = gdf1, print.progress = FALSE, iter = 0)
fit1 <- lm.rrpp(shape ~ log(CS), SS.type = "I",
               data = gdf1, print.progress = FALSE, iter = 0)

gdf2 <- geomorph.data.frame(shape = as.matrix(fit1$LM$residuals), Sex = Pupfish$Sex)
fit2 <- lm.rrpp(shape ~ Sex, SS.type = "I",
               data = gdf2, print.progress = FALSE, iter = 0)

coef(fit, test = TRUE)
coef(fit1, test = TRUE)
coef(fit2, test = TRUE)

For fit:
d.obs UCL (95%) Zd Pr(>d) log(CS) 0.11094067 0.10286076 1.360292 0.3333333 SexM 0.02754004 0.02597288 1.285267 0.3333333

For fit1:
d.obs UCL (95%) Zd Pr(>d) log(CS) 0.1109407 0.1028608 1.360292 0.3333333

Since I used type I sum of square, Sex coefficients from fit and fit2 should be identical. Why this is not the case?

Regarding your questions

> On Mar 14, 2023, at 4:27 AM, lv xiao <lxi...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> While the coefficient for log(CS) is 0.11094067 in both fit and fit1, there is some slight difference between the coefficients for Sex in fit and fit2. Since I used type I sum of square, Sex coefficients from fit and fit2 should be identical. Why this is not the case?

No, the coefficient should not be the same in each case.  Try using reveal.model.designs on each fit and you will learn that the reduced models differ in each case for Sex based on your set-up, even if inadvertently you did not create different reduced models for log(CS).

> My 2nd question is if this is to be expected or I made mistakes anywhere in my code?

Of course it is to be expected.  The residuals have the mean shape plus other effects subtracted from the original data.  You took the mean on residuals that have a mean of 0, 0, 0, …  You plotted a cluster of residuals missing the mean shape so it would be silly to expect the mean shape is there.

> I may wish to learn how large iter should normally be set and if there is a way to substantially accelerate lm.rrpp?

Just as a check for a set of data with 2,000 specimens and 21,000 variables, here is the object size I find:

> Y <- matrix(rnorm(2000 * 21000), 2000, 21000)
> object.size(Y)
336000216 bytes

That is 336 megabytes.  Couple that with the size of linear model design matrices and there are some very large objects to use in every calculation in every iteration.  However, most of the time spent when iter = 0 is for overhead tasks that do not need to be repeated in every iteration.  So you probably should not expect that you multiply 30 minutes times 1000 as an expected timeframe.  Nevertheless, asking for analyses to be completed in one hour, even with a very large computer, might be unreasonable.

Here are some things to realize.

1. Parallel processing with a Windows machine is not as ideal.  Sorry, but it is more efficient with a Unix environment (Mac or Linux).  Maybe the high performance computer is not Windows based?
2. Parallel processing is not always faster if the overhead of splitting tasks among cores supersedes the capacity of each core to do the task.  (The high performance computer might have little issue with this.)
3. If you only need to do ANOVA — do not have perform tests on coefficients — then using turbo = TRUE will help immensely.
4. Parallel = TRUE only applies to the iterative part of your analysis, so if iter = 0, no parallel processing was performed in your assessment.  The time you experienced was only for lm.rrpp overhead, which involves a PCA, obtaining linear model design matrices, performing several QR decompositions, and bundling various large objects in order to perform RRPP.  You should compare this time to the time it would take to perform a few iterations to get an idea of how long it will take.  It’s a lot like preparing a nice dinner.  Sometimes the preparation takes a long time but everyone then eats fast!

Best,
Mike

> Is it because in the 2B-pPLS we take the phylogenetic relationship of the different primates into account?

Yes.

One might say that the significant (not really positive even if the line looks like that) relationship when not taking phylogeny into account is spurious, because the observations are not independent.  The expectation is that species with more recent evolutionary divergence have more correlated shapes, so accounting for that auto-correlation in a PGLS analysis is why the result is less correlated.  An alternative explanation is that evolutionary divergence is constrained along an integrated axis of shape and function.  Anatomical changes that result in improper function are not likely to evolve.   Accounting for phylogeny in 2B-PLS might reveal the subtle, novel evolutionary directions species take, independent of the anatomical constraint. > > > Is there a way to include a single landmark in multiple modules or do I need to make some decisions about what landmarks to assign to a single module?
>
> I am really happy this question was asked!  I am happy because it leads to a similar topic that I think needs to be discussed.  If you wish to avoid a soapbox moment from me, please stop reading now.
>
> In his 2019 paper, Cardini advocated for performing separate GPAs on modules before testing for modularity or integration, to reduce the risk of spurious integration and modularity signals in shape data, that seems to arise from GPA.  (I would posit that covariances that suggest modularity or integration probably have a physical spatial signal that is not purely induced by GPA but following this topic would be a digression from the present one.)  It was a convenience in the examples considered that landmarks fell into separate modules but like Madlen’s example, maybe landmarks are found at the border of putative modules (like sutures of skull bones) and it is difficult to define the modules (separate bone shapes) without re-using landmarks in separate modules.  As Dean pointed out, this is a limitation, but one might argue that it isn’t, if Cardini’s (2019) approach is used?
>
> Tests of modularity basically involve constructing a covariance matrix and partitioning it into symmetric blocks (covariances within modules) and asymmetric blocks (covariance between modules).  Tests statistics either focus on the asymmetric blocks or the strength of covariation in these blocks relative to within the module blocks.  If the same landmarks — and therefore, their coordinates as variables — are found in separate module blocks, there is a corresponding between-module covariance in the asymmetric block for each variable.  As you know, the correlation between a variable and itself is perfectly 1.  Populating this between-module block with covariances of perfectly correlated variables will inflate the correlation between modules, thus inflating the apparent integration (and potentially reducing the strength of modularity).  So even if this could be done by manipulating two.b.pls for a test of integration, it would be a spurious result.  Luckily this is not something that can be as easily finagled with modularity.test, since only one matrix or array is input (one would have to duplicate landmarks to make it work).
>
> But what if one performed separate GPAs on modules, both containing some of the same landmarks, like two separate skull bones sharing a suture?  Now the correlations between them would not be perfectly 1, because the variables are no longer the same even if they are coordinates for the same landmarks.  With several landmarks — say 3 or 4 along the same suture line — there would still be high correlation between the same landmarks in separate modules, as well as those 3-4 landmarks within modules, as well as all of the possible pairs of 3 or 4 landmarks between modules.  This is to say, one still produces a spurious result, but now with the addition of actually altering the real spatial covariances of landmarks on the skull (as found between the contrived modules) with their artificial duplication.  To put it bluntly, this is asinine.
>
> But is it okay then to perform separate GPAs as long as the modules do not contain the same landmarks?  No!  No!  No!  The principle is the same.  One is artificially altering the (presumptively) real covariances that exist between landmarks because of their real spatial locations.  The skull bones cannot be disassembled from the skull if one is evaluating the modularity or integration of putative skull modules, if the skull morphology as defined by the netire configuration is to mean anything.
>
> I implore people to not do separate GPAs and if you feel compelled by reviewers of your manuscript to add that analysis, maybe consider pulling this email from the archives as a rebuttal.  Madlen’s question offers a perfect illustration of why tests of modularity and integration with GM data should not use separate GPAs.  That the modules copuld include the same anatomical references points and in the process their true spatial covariances would be rendered meaningless if a far larger problem than performing separate GPAs could solve.
>
> Madlen, if I were in your shoes, I would take the two modules and make them three: the two previous modules without the shared landmarks and one module for the landmarks they share.  If nothing else, you can learn how integrated these landmarks are with either module.
>
> Cheers!

Hi Madlen,

based on the summary of your fit.unique model I think there is a significance different in allometry between at least some groups. To be more certain though I would also need to see the results of the ANOVA you ran to compare fit.unique and fit.common. When I do my own allometry analysis, I also add to the ANOVA a simple common allometry null model (shape ~ size) with no covariates to clear any doubt and check that the models with  covariates are indeed better than the common slope model.

Assuming that fit.unique is indeed the best model, then to perform a pairwise test on the slopes using the RRPP package you need to slightly change the formula. You will need to add size (logCS) as a covariate as indicated in the help file for the function:
covariate

A numeric vector for which to calculate slopes for comparison If NULL, LS means will be calculated instead of slopes.

Currently you are testing for the difference in LS means which is not equivalent. Also, I prefer to indicate a fit.null model in the formula. I usually use a model like your fit.common model as the null is the ANOVA shows that is significantly different from the simple common allometry model without covariates.

After you performed the pairwise test, you can easily obtain both absolute differences and angular differences between the slopes using the summary function.

You can find all the details on this and the reasoning behind using a covariate in the pairwise help file:

https://rdrr.io/cran/RRPP/man/pairwise.html

Hope this helps!

Agnese

I have a question regarding using na.omit.

I am using na.omit function to extract shape data from a data frame that includes more sample than I have represented in my phylogeny. But I am having trouble when I include more information in this new data frame. Here is my code:

classifiers.all  <- read.csv(file="classifiers_inGPAorder.csv", row.names = 1)
dim(classifiers.all)
[1] 62 11
nwt.tree <- read.tree("NWTfinal_renamedtoclassifiersGPAall.tre")
plot(nwt.tree)

SM.output<-parser(file.choose(), forceLPS = TRUE)
dim(SM.output$LM)
[1] 46 3 62

Y.gpa<-gpagen(SM.output$LM, verbose = TRUE)
gdf <- geomorph.data.frame(Y.gpa)
gdf$d <- Y.gpa$procD
gdf$group <- c(classifiers.all$Include)
gdf
ndf <- na.omit(gdf)
ndf

classifiers.red  <- read.csv(file="classifiers_inGPAorder_red.csv", row.names = 1)
dim(classifiers.red)
[1] 39 10
chk <- name.check(nwt.tree, classifiers.red)
chk
[1] "OK"
ndf.final <- geomorph.data.frame(ndf, species = classifiers.red$Species, genus = classifiers.red$Genus, elevation = classifiers.red$Elevation, temp = classifiers.red$Temp, precip = classifiers.red$Prec, lat = classifiers.red$Longitude, lon = classifiers.red$Latitude, phy = nwt.tree)

> model1 <- procD.pgls(coords ~ log(Csize), phy = phy, data = ndf.final, iter = 999) Error: Data names and covariance matrix names do not match.

I appreciate any help and suggestions to solve this error.

Thank you!
Julia
